title: Servo motor control
desc: Potentiometer steers servo to any position
content_html:
Materials

  • 1 x Arduino Uno (or compatible board) (Nerokas - nerokas.co.ke)
  • 1 x SG90 micro servo motor (Pixel Electronics - pixelelectronics.co.ke)
  • 1 x 10k ohm rotary potentiometer (Nerokas - nerokas.co.ke)
  • 1 x Breadboard (half-size or full-size) (Nerokas - nerokas.co.ke)
  • 1 x USB cable (A to B, matching the Arduino board) (Pixel Electronics - pixelelectronics.co.ke)
  • 7 x Male-to-male jumper wires (Nerokas - nerokas.co.ke)
  • 1 x Small screwdriver or plastic servo horn arm (usually included with servo) (Pixel Electronics - pixelelectronics.co.ke)
  • 1 x Laptop/computer with Arduino IDE installed (not purchased locally)
  • Optional: 1 x external 5V power supply for the servo if using a larger/higher-torque servo (Nerokas - nerokas.co.ke)

How It Works

A potentiometer is a knob that changes how much electricity can flow through it as you turn it. Inside the Arduino, an Analog-to-Digital Converter reads the voltage coming from the potentiometer and turns it into a number between 0 and 1023. When the knob is turned all the way one way, the number is close to 0. Turned all the way the other way, the number is close to 1023. Anywhere in between gives a number in between.

A servo motor is a special motor that can turn to an exact angle and then hold that position, instead of spinning around and around like a normal motor. You tell it what angle to go to (between 0 and 180 degrees) by sending it a signal, and it moves there and stops.

In this project, we connect the potentiometer's output to one of the Arduino's analog input pins, and we connect the servo's signal wire to one of the Arduino's digital pins. The Arduino constantly checks the potentiometer's number (0-1023) and converts it into a servo angle (0-180 degrees) using a built-in math function called map(). It then tells the servo to move to that exact angle. Because this happens many times per second, turning the knob feels like you are directly steering the servo with your hand - the servo becomes a "dial" you can point anywhere you like.

This teaches two big ideas at once: reading an analog sensor (the potentiometer) and controlling an actuator (the servo) based on that sensor's value - the foundation of almost every robot and smart device.

Step-by-Step Instructions

  1. Place the potentiometer on the breadboard so its three legs each sit in a different row.
  2. Connect the potentiometer's left leg to the Arduino's 5V pin using a jumper wire.
  3. Connect the potentiometer's right leg to the Arduino's GND pin using a jumper wire.
  4. Connect the potentiometer's middle leg (the wiper, which gives the changing voltage) to Arduino analog pin A0.
  5. Place the servo near the breadboard. Note its three wires: usually brown/black (ground), red (power), and orange/yellow (signal).
  6. Connect the servo's brown/black wire to the Arduino's GND pin (you can share the same GND rail as the potentiometer).
  7. Connect the servo's red wire to the Arduino's 5V pin.
  8. Connect the servo's orange/yellow signal wire to Arduino digital pin 9.
  9. Double-check all connections before plugging in the USB cable - point out that GND must be shared between the potentiometer and the servo for the circuit to work correctly.
  10. Open the Arduino IDE, plug in the Arduino via USB, and select the correct board and port under the Tools menu.
  11. Type or paste the full code from the "Full Code" section below into a new sketch.
  12. Click Upload. Students should see the "TX/RX" lights blink briefly, then no errors in the black console at the bottom.
  13. Slowly turn the potentiometer knob. Ask students to observe: the servo horn should rotate smoothly to follow the knob's position.
  14. Open Tools > Serial Monitor (set to 9600 baud) so students can see the raw potentiometer reading and the calculated servo angle printed live as they turn the knob.
  15. Turn the knob fully in each direction and ask students to note the minimum and maximum angle values shown (should be close to 0 and 180).
  16. Optional: attach a pointer or arm to the servo horn so the "steering" effect is visually obvious, like a needle on a dial.

Full Code

#include <Servo.h>   // Library that makes controlling servo motors easy

Servo myServo;              // Create a Servo object to control our servo
int potPin = A0;             // Potentiometer wiper is connected to analog pin A0
int servoPin = 9;             // Servo signal wire is connected to digital pin 9

int potValue = 0;             // Will store the raw reading from the potentiometer (0-1023)
int servoAngle = 0;             // Will store the converted angle for the servo (0-180)

void setup() {
  myServo.attach(servoPin);   // Tell the Servo library which pin to send signals to
  Serial.begin(9600);           // Start Serial communication so we can watch values on the computer
}

void loop() {
  potValue = analogRead(potPin);   // Read the potentiometer: gives a number from 0 to 1023

  // Convert the 0-1023 range into a 0-180 range that servos understand
  servoAngle = map(potValue, 0, 1023, 0, 180);

  myServo.write(servoAngle);   // Command the servo to move to the calculated angle

  // Print both values so students can see the relationship live
  Serial.print("Potentiometer: ");
  Serial.print(potValue);          // Show the raw analog reading
  Serial.print("   Servo Angle: ");
  Serial.println(servoAngle);      // Show the angle sent to the servo, then start a new line

  delay(15);   // Small pause gives the servo time to move smoothly and stops jittery readings
}

Common Mistakes & Fixes

SymptomLikely CauseFix
Servo does not move at allSignal wire connected to the wrong pin, or servo library not attached correctlyConfirm the orange/yellow wire is on digital pin 9 and that servoPin in code matches the physical pin used
Servo jitters or shakes constantlyNot enough power reaching the servo, especially if powered directly from the Arduino's 5V pin along with other componentsReduce other current draw, add a small delay in the loop, or use an external 5V supply for the servo
Potentiometer reading stays at 0 or 1023 no matter how it's turnedWiper (middle leg) not connected to A0, or 5V/GND wires swappedRe-check that the middle leg goes to A0, and outer legs go to 5V and GND respectively
Serial Monitor shows scrambled or no textBaud rate mismatch between code and Serial MonitorSet Serial Monitor's baud rate dropdown to 9600 to match Serial.begin(9600) in the code
Servo moves but only within a small range, not full 0-180Potentiometer wiring loose or potentiometer only physically turns through part of its range being usedCheck connections are firm, and confirm students are turning the knob through its full rotation
Upload fails with a "port not found" or similar errorWrong board or port selected in Arduino IDE, or USB cable is faulty/charge-onlyCheck Tools > Board and Tools > Port settings, and try a different USB cable

Discussion Questions

  • What number range does analogRead() give us, and why do you think that specific range was chosen?
  • Why do we need the map() function in this project? What would happen if we sent the raw potentiometer value straight to the servo?
  • Can you think of a real-world device that uses a dial or knob to control something's position, similar to this project?
  • Why do the potentiometer and the servo both need to be connected to the same GND pin?
  • What do you think would happen if we removed the delay(15); line from the code? Would you expect a difference, and why?

Extension Challenges

  • Easy: Add a second potentiometer and second servo, so students control two servos independently with two knobs on the same breadboard.
  • Medium: Modify the code so the servo only moves in steps of 10 degrees (e.g., 0, 10, 20...180) instead of smoothly, and explain why the movement looks different.
  • Hard: Add an LED that lights up only when the servo angle is within a specific "target zone" (for example, between 80 and 100 degrees), turning this into a simple aiming or calibration game.
